title: Alerting Design
summary: Writing alerts that page the right person for the right reason, and structuring the response path around them.

slides.markdown:
Alerts differ in *what triggers them* and this changes everything downstream.

| Style | Triggers on | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Symptom-based | What users actually feel | "Error rate above 2%" |
| Cause-based | An internal condition that might or might not affect users | "CPU above 80%" |

**How to decide:** alert primarily on symptoms — they only fire when something user-facing is actually wrong. Cause-based alerts fire on internal conditions that are often benign (high CPU during a scheduled batch job) and train people to ignore pages.

Every page should come with an implicit or explicit answer to "what do I do right now?" An alert that fires but has no clear next step just produces stress with no path to resolution — the on-call engineer stares at a symptom with no idea whether to restart something, roll back, or escalate.

A useful test before shipping any new alert: could two different on-call engineers, both paged at 3am, take the same first action from this alert alone? If not, it needs a runbook link or it needs to not page at all.

**Alert fatigue** is what happens when too many low-value pages erode the quality of every response — an engineer paged five times a night for things that turned out to be nothing starts responding slower, more skeptically, and eventually starts silencing or ignoring pages altogether, including the one time it's real.

Fatigue is a direct consequence of over-alerting on causes instead of symptoms, and of setting thresholds too sensitively "just to be safe." Cutting alert *volume* deliberately is often the single highest-leverage on-call improvement a team can make.

Not every alert deserves the same urgency channel. **Paging** (waking someone up) should be reserved for things that need action *now* — active user impact. A **ticket** fits something real but not urgent — fix it next business day. A **chat** notification suits FYI-level signals nobody needs to act on immediately.

Misrouting urgency in either direction is costly: paging for a ticket-level issue burns trust and causes fatigue; ticketing something that's actually actively hurting users delays response when speed mattered most.

A **runbook** is the documented, step-by-step response for a specific alert — check X, if Y then do Z, escalate to this team if it doesn't resolve. Linking every alert to its runbook is what turns "actionable" from an aspiration into a fact: a half-asleep engineer doesn't have to reconstruct the right response from memory at 3am.

Runbooks decay if untouched — the fix that worked six months ago may no longer apply after an architecture change, so a stale runbook that leads to the wrong action is arguably worse than no runbook at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Rewriting a noisy CPU alert into a symptom-based one
slides.markdown:
Worked example: a team pages on "CPU above 80% for 5 minutes," which fires constantly during expected batch jobs and rarely correlates with any actual user impact — classic alert fatigue in progress. The fix: replace it with "error rate above 2% for 5 minutes" and "p99 latency above 2 seconds for 5 minutes," both measuring what users would actually feel.

The old CPU metric doesn't disappear — it moves to a dashboard for root-causing an active incident, but it stops being what wakes someone up.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: what makes a good alert
slides.markdown: A clean way to structure this in an interview: a good alert is **symptom-based** (fires on what users feel, not an internal proxy), **actionable** (the page implies or links a clear next step), and **tuned to avoid fatigue** (rare enough that every page is trusted). Miss any one of the three and the alert either doesn't fire when it should, fires and nobody knows what to do, or fires so often it gets ignored.

slides.subTitle: Catching a slow burn without paging on noise
slides.markdown:
A naive SLO alert — "error rate above 1% for 5 minutes" — either fires on brief blips that self-resolve, or misses a slower, sustained problem that stays just under the 5-minute threshold's reset. **Multi-window, multi-burn-rate** alerting fixes both: it pages only when error budget is burning too fast across *two* windows at once — a short window (5 minutes, catches fast severe outages) **and** a long window (1 hour, catches sustained moderate ones) both must exceed their burn-rate threshold.

Requiring both windows to agree is what suppresses noise from a brief blip (fails the long window) while still catching a slow leak (fails the long window even though the short window looks calm at any given instant). This is the technique behind Google SRE's standard SLO-based paging.

slides.subTitle: An alert that flaps instead of firing cleanly
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "the threshold is right, so the alert will behave correctly."

**Why it breaks:** a metric hovering right at the threshold — error rate oscillating between 1.8% and 2.1% against a 2% alert — causes the alert to fire, resolve, fire, resolve every few minutes. Each transition often re-pages, so on-call gets hammered by the same underlying issue dozens of times, which is its own form of alert fatigue distinct from too-sensitive thresholds.

**The correct model:** add hysteresis — a different (lower) threshold to resolve than to fire, or require the condition to hold for a sustained window before either firing or clearing — so an alert transitions cleanly instead of flapping around a boundary value.
